facts.statement: Zhongornis was found in the Yixian Formation in Lingyuan City, China, and was described by Gao et al. in 2008.
facts.quote: It was found in rocks of the Yixian Formation in Lingyuan City (China), and described by Gao et al. in 2008.

facts.statement: The only described species of Zhongornis is Zhongornis haoae.
facts.quote: Zhongornis has only one described species, Zhongornis haoae.

facts.statement: The Zhongornis specimen is housed in the Dalian Natural History Museum.
facts.quote: It is in the collection of the Dalian Natural History Museum.

facts.statement: The Zhongornis fossil is a fairly complete skeleton approximately eight centimeters long.
facts.quote: It is a fairly complete skeleton about eight centimeters in length.

facts.statement: Feather impressions are preserved on the right hand and probable tail feathers are near the left foot of the Zhongornis specimen.
facts.quote: There are feather impressions preserved on the right hand and also probable tail feathers preserved near the left foot.

facts.statement: Zhongornis had a beaked mouth without teeth.
facts.quote: Zhongornis had a beaked mouth with no teeth.

facts.statement: Zhongornis had a proportionately short tail with thirteen vertebrae and no pygostyle.
facts.quote: The tail is proportionately short, has thirteen vertebrae, and no pygostyle.

facts.statement: The third finger of Zhongornis has only two phalangeal bones, a trait shared with Enantiornithes and advanced avialans but not non-avian dinosaurs or Confuciusornis.
facts.quote: The third finger has only two phalangeal bones, unlike non-avian dinosaurs and Confuciusornis, and more like Enantiornithes and more advanced avialans.

facts.statement: Zhongornis provides key anatomical evidence for the evolutionary transition from primitive basal Avialae with long tails to advanced avialans with fused tails.
facts.quote: Zhongornis provides important anatomical information about the evolutionary transition from primitive basal Avialae like Archaeopteryx, which had a long bony tail and a dinosaur-like third finger, to the more advanced avialans like the Enantiornithes, which had reduced third fingers and tails fused into rigid pygostyles.

facts.statement: Zhongornis has only thirteen caudal vertebrae, significantly fewer than the twenty-two found in Archaeopteryx.
facts.quote: It has only thirteen caudal vertebrae, far less than the 22 in Archaeopteryx.

facts.statement: Although the vertebral centra are not fused, the last four form a continuous lateral flange, implying the specimen had an incipient pygostyle.
facts.quote: None of the vertebral centra are fused, but the last four do form a continuous lateral flange, implying that this specimen had an incipient pygostyle.

facts.statement: Other phylogenetic analyses reject the hypothesis that Zhongornis is a scansoriopterygid, instead placing it as a primitive relative of pygostylians or a close relative of Confuciusornis.
facts.quote: Other phylogenetic analyses, including a larger dataset, don't consider the hypothesis that Zhongornis is a scansoriopterygid, instead finding it in its traditional position as a primitive relative of pygostylians, or as a close relative of Confuciusornis.

facts.statement: Some researchers consider the scansoriopterygid hypothesis invalid because Zhongornis differs strongly from that group in many traits it shares with birds.
facts.quote: Some researchers consider the scansoriopterygid hypothesis invalid, as they believe Zhongornis strongly differs from this group in many traits, traits that it also shares with birds.

facts.statement: Zhongornis lived during the Barremian to Aptian stages, approximately 125.77 to 119.57 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Aptian (125.77 to 119.57 million years ago)
